newsitem.title: UK: Short stg seen holding promise despite rate rise.
newsitem.headline: Short stg seen holding promise despite rate rise.

text.p: British interest rate futures still offer value despite Thursday's quarter point rise in official British rates, analysts said.
"The initial reaction on the short sterling curve is probably positive," said Kit Juckes, head of bond and currency strategy at NatWest Capital Markets in London.
"The striking feature is that the curve has the potential to steepen so that the front end will outperform."
The Bank of England's monetary policy committee raised interest rates by 25 basis points to 6.75 percent on Thursday.
At 1153 GMT December short sterling futures were at 92.60, up five basis points on the day and little changed from their position before the announcement.
This implies three-month money rates of around 7.4 percent by the end of the year, suggesting official rates of around 7.25 percent.
"I still think interest rates will be at seven percent by the end of the year," said Juckes.
"The likelihood is people will wonder how much more there is to go for and to that extent the curve will probably steepen."
The December contract was at 92.59 just before the Bank raised rates and climbed immediately to 92.65 before slipping lower to 92.54 and then recovering.
The 1998 contracts dipped slightly after the announcement with March at 92.47 and June at 92.45, both up two basis points on the day. September 1998 futures were up 0.03 at 92.47.
Analysts said there had been some expectations of an increase of 50 basis points on interest rates and the short sterling market had firmed on the relief.
"There was certainly a risk of a more aggressive move," said Tom Rayner, ecnomist at Societe Generale Strauss Turnbull in London.
He said the Bank of England's mention of the strength of sterling and the "contractionary effects of the recent budget" had possibly kept the increase to 25 basis points.

"But we don't think the budget will have such a big impact on the personal sector which is where the real fears come through, so we still see further rate rises ahead," he said adding that he saw base rates at 7.25 by the end of the year.
"The peak in rates is probably going to be around 7.5 percent in terms of base rates and three-month LIBOR may have to go above that before it levels out and starts to head down again," said Rayner.
He said the mid-1998 contracts could offer some selling opportunites as they might not be discounting a high enough peak in interest rates.
David Bloom, UK economist at HSBC James Capel also saw interest rates at 7.25 by the end of 1997 and said there would be more rate increases further out.
"We'll be looking for a peak of about eight percent by late 1998," he said, but added that much depended on what happened to sterling.
"Unless sterling comes off, then I think we'll see rates go up sharper than we're anticipating," he said.
"And given interest rate differentials are driving sterling, it's very difficult to see why sterling should come of at the moment."
